transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 9 to 13.

transcript.speaker: Greg
transcript.text: Natalie, have you finished your outline for the report we've been assigned? You know, the one about the biology field trip to Hawthorne Oceanic Research Facility.

transcript.text: Hi Greg, I'm still thinking about what topic to focus on. I thought maybe the subject of symbiosis.

transcript.speaker: Greg
transcript.text: Oh yes, I remember that the chapter about it in our textbook was really fascinating, particularly the symbiotic relationships involving cleaner fish, like the rasfish we studied.

transcript.speaker: Natalie
transcript.text: And there were moray eels at the Hawthorne facilities, as well as rasfish. I can describe in detail the cleaning process between those two species.

transcript.speaker: Greg
transcript.text: What did that involve again?

transcript.speaker: Natalie
transcript.text: Well, the moray eels and rasfish were in the same tank living on a reef. The rasfish gathered inside the reef and hung around until other fish showed up.

transcript.speaker: Greg
transcript.text: Ah, I remember. The eels went there to be cleaned.

transcript.speaker: Natalie
transcript.text: Yes, Mr Horace explained that.

transcript.speaker: Greg
transcript.text: He did. He said they usually gathered together near the cleaning station.

transcript.speaker: Natalie
transcript.text: Yeah, and then the rasfish would approach the moray eels there while they were resting. And that's when they would start the cleaning process.
transcript.highlight_text: approach the moray eels there while they were resting.

transcript.speaker: Greg
transcript.text: Right, I remember. First they clean up the eels' gills by eating parasites and bacteria.
transcript.highlight_text: clean up the eels' gills by eating parasites and bacteria.

transcript.text: Yes, they actually eat that stuff right off the eels. And they pick away the dead scales as well.
transcript.highlight_text: they pick away the dead scales as well.

transcript.speaker: Greg
transcript.text: Actually, you might also want to mention that the eels really rely on the fish because the parasites they eat are quite dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Natalie
transcript.text: Also, at the end, the moray eels would often open their mouths and let the rasfish swim inside to clean as well. I thought it was really fascinating to see that part of the process.
transcript.highlight_text: the moray eels would often open their mouths and let the rasfish swim inside to clean

transcript.speaker: Natalie
transcript.text: Now, all I have to do is come up with some other examples of symbiotic relationships.

transcript.speaker: Greg
transcript.text: Check out the list of references on Mr Horace's course outline. I'm sure you can find something suitable on it.
